name: Amorite
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Streck, M. P. 2000. Das amurritische Onomastikon der altbabylonischen Zeit (named in Wikipedia refs I loaded); Waltisberg 2011 (Glottolog MED) is on case, not prosody. Corpus is personal names only; stress likely unrecoverable.

sources.citation: Bauer, Theo. 1926. Die Ostkanaanäer. Eine philologisch-historische Untersuchung über die Wanderschicht der sogenannten "Amoriter" in Babylonien. Leipzig: Asia Major.
sources.note: Only incidental: p. 7 'Denn bitti ist das Femini[n]um zu bin und gleich dem hebr. bat, nur daß hier nach dem Philippischen Lautgesetz das betonte i zu a geworden ist' (Philippi's law applied to the Hebrew cognate); no statement of where Amorite stress falls.
Nothing on stress; used only for its reference list (George & Krebernik 2022, Golinets 2025, Ross 2025).

sources.citation: Golinets, Viktor. 2025. "The Significance of the Newly Found Amorite-Akkadian Bilinguals for Hebrew Lexicography." In Hornkohl et al. (eds.), Interconnected Traditions: A Festschrift for Geoffrey Khan, vol. 1, 879-900. Cambridge: Open Book Publishers. doi:10.11647/obp.0463.32
sources.note: Lexical comparison with Hebrew; nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Buccellati, Giorgio. 1997. "Akkadian and Amorite Phonology." In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa (Including the Caucasus), vol. 1, 3-38. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
sources.note: Sec. 1.3.7 'Suprasegmentals' (pp. 23-24): 'All consonants and vowels can be lengthened in Akkadian and Amorite'; stress is then discussed ONLY for Akkadian ('The traditional view about Akkadian stress is that it falls on the first long syllable from the end of the word...'). No statement about Amorite stress anywhere; sec. 1.3.9 mentions stress (Aro 1953) again only for post-Old-Akkadian dialects of Akkadian.

sources.citation: Buccellati, Giorgio. 1996. "Amorite." In Jane Turner (ed.), The Dictionary of Art, vol. 1. London: Macmillan/Grove.
